chapter: Wagon bands, halls and the old brass bands
title: Grandfather Barbarin, the hearse driver Joe Never Smile
summary: His grandfather played mellophone and alto horn, drove carriages and hearses, and never smiled or moved at funerals.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line

blocks.x: What did he play, your grandfather, Danny?

Mellophone and alto horn. He had played trumpet to begin with, but they told him to get off the trumpet. But he was just about as Creole as you could get. He used to eat dinner every day at 12 o'clock with his bottle of wine. He was French as you... He'd never say nothin'. He never said nothing, except (?)"If Negroes start a fight or something, they're lucky to (?)."(?) Didn't move a muscle. He was the first... He drove... He was a carriage-driver, which was a profession in the South.

A hackman. And he drove the hearse for the undertaking parlors. They called him "Joe Never Smile." Sit on this hearse... You had to have this beaver or this derby, and you'd sit on a hearse, and you had to not get emotionally aroused by nothin', because you had them kind of funerals where the wives and everybody go hysterical and they start screamin' and howlin' and runnin', and then
breaking up the place because they just closed the casket, and they come out and there's pandemonium. So Grandpa said, "don't never smile, never move a muscle."
Just sat there. That was Paul Barbarin's father, right?

His attitude was be cold! [DISSOLVES IN LAUGHTER]... Stay cold! No matter how much a woman screams. "Oh! My baby's gone. My husband's gone. My mother's gone. Lawd, they done closed that casket! I don't care what happens." "Don't never smile, don't move a muscle." And he'd tell his horses. He'd go, CLIP-CLOP, hit them horses on the rump with them lines (?), and the hearse would pull off. Don't move a muscle.
Three undertaking parlors he worked -- funerals. Always, most of the time with that hearse.
